newsitem.title: USA: Meat, vegetables, coffee may boost US food prices.
newsitem.headline: Meat, vegetables, coffee may boost US food prices.

text.p: Meat, fresh vegetables and coffee are three commodities that might upset government forecasts of modest food price increases this year, Agriculture Department economist Annette Clauson said Tuesday.

U.S. food prices will rise 2.5 percent to three percent during 1997, according to a revised forecast issued as part of the department's annual Outlook Forum. They rose 3.3 percent last year, the largest increase since 1990's 5.8 percent.
During a panel discussion, Clauson painted a generally benign picture for price pressure this year. Most commodities would rise two percent to four percent, she said.
However, Clauson said meat, fresh vegetables and coffee were the commodities that could confound the outlook.
Sluggish beef exports have helped keep domestic meat prices steady. If exports pick up, it could mean higher prices in the grocery store.

The aftermath of winter storms may delay planting of spring vegetables in California, she said. If delays are widespread, there could be "some gaps" in supply. Prices usually spike upward during such temporary shortages.
Wholesale coffee prices have risen on concern about production in Brazil and Colombia.

At present, the department estimates that prices for nonalcoholic beverages, the sector including coffee, will rise two percent to four percent this year. The rise in wholesale prices may translate into higher retail prices.
